topic: refitting the floor and ramp of a two-horse trailer before the season

provenance.author: glowny-en-c
provenance.notes: 10 turns, user first; variant a is a timber and screw order for the same refit with closed task questions, base is a diagnostic talk about a soft floor and a banging ramp. Grounded external referent: the ramp, introduced in turn 0 and mentioned in the sentence directly before every insertion (it takes the horses' weight, its hinge line and springs are suspects, its boards are part of the order).

a: The trailer refit needs a timber order, and the floor comes first on the sheet.
The floor takes fifteen boards, and every board runs two point four metres in length.
The ramp takes eight boards, and every ramp board runs one point five metres.
Work out the total length of board for the floor and then for the ramp.
How many metres of board does the whole order come to across both parts?
base: Our two-horse trailer failed its yearly check because the floor felt soft near the back edge.
We lifted the rubber mats and found dark wet boards where the floor meets the ramp.
The ramp drops with a bang now, and the horses hesitate on it every single time.
Under the ramp the hinge line is stained with rust and one spring looks stretched.
Where would you start so the trailer is safe well before the season begins?

a: The floor comes to thirty-six metres of board at fifteen boards of two point four.
The ramp comes to twelve metres of board at eight boards of one point five.
Across both parts the whole order stands at forty-eight metres of board in total.
Each floor board needs six screws and each ramp board needs four screws.
Does a count of ninety screws for the floor match the number on your sheet?
base: Start with the boards, because soft timber near the back edge spreads faster than people expect.
Press a blunt key along each board and mark every spot where the point sinks in.
Then look at the ramp, since a ramp that bangs down usually means a tired spring.
A stretched spring throws the whole weight of the ramp onto your arms and the hinge line.
How old are the springs, and have they ever been changed since you bought it?

a: Now price the timber at ten pounds for every metre of board on the order.
Give the floor cost and the ramp cost and then the figure for both together.
The screws come in boxes of fifty, and no box may be split at the counter.
Work out how many boxes cover one hundred twenty-two screws and what is left over.
Which single figure goes on the order line for the timber across both parts?
base: The springs are the ones the trailer came with, so they are at least twelve years old.
I pressed the key along the floor and marked eleven soft spots by the back edge.
The ramp boards look better, though two of them are dark along the hinge line.
Nothing sank in anywhere near the front half, which stayed dry under the mats.
Would you replace the whole floor, or only the run of boards that failed the key?

a: The floor timber costs three hundred sixty pounds at thirty-six metres and ten pounds the metre.
The ramp timber costs one hundred twenty pounds at twelve metres on the same rate.
The order line for timber across both parts reads four hundred eighty pounds.
Three boxes of fifty cover one hundred twenty-two screws with twenty-eight screws left over.
Does the spare count of twenty-eight match the margin you wanted for the job?
base: Replace the whole run from the back edge to the axle line, not just the marked boards.
Mixed old and new boards flex differently, and the join between them becomes the next weak spot.
On the ramp I would change the two dark boards and both springs in one go.
New springs will let the ramp rise gently instead of dropping its weight on you.
Can you get the trailer under cover for a week while the boards are out?

a: One correction has come in from the yard before the order goes off today.
The ramp boards run one point six metres each, not one point five as listed.
Rework the ramp length, the ramp cost, and the totals that change with them.
Leave the floor figures alone, because that part of the sheet was checked twice.
What is the new total length of board across both parts of the order?
base: The trailer can sit in the barn for two weeks, so time is not the problem.
My worry is choosing the timber, because the last owner clearly got that wrong.
The ramp boards outlasted the floor by years, so whatever went into the ramp was tougher.
The failed floor boards are plain softwood without any treatment stamp anywhere on them.
Which timber would you buy so the new floor outlasts the next owner as well?

a: The ramp now comes to twelve point eight metres at eight boards of one point six.
The ramp timber cost moves to one hundred twenty-eight pounds on the ten pound rate.
The total length of board across both parts becomes forty-eight point eight metres.
The timber order line moves to four hundred eighty-eight pounds with the floor unchanged.
Is the screw count still right, or do the longer boards take extra fixings?
base: Buy pressure treated boards for the floor, and ask the yard for the heavy duty grade.
Treated timber shrugs off the wet that horses bring in on their feet every trip.
For the ramp, match the thickness of the old boards so the hinge line sits flush.
A ramp board that stands proud catches hooves, and a low one lets water pool.
While the yard cuts your order, shall we plan the strip down step by step?

a: The yard confirms that the longer ramp boards take five screws each instead of four.
Rework the screw total and the box count on the fifty to a box rule.
Then set out the job across four days from Monday to Thursday in order.
Day one is the strip down and day two is the frame check and treatment.
How many screws does the full order need now across floor and ramp together?
base: Yes, give me the strip down in order, because I have never opened a trailer floor.
I have a long weekend free, and my neighbour can lend a hand on Saturday.
The only tools in the barn are a drill, a saw, and a box of clamps.
The mats are heavy but they roll up, so the two of us can shift them.
Is there anything under the boards that a careless bar could wreck on the way?

a: The ramp now needs forty screws and the floor stays at ninety screws.
The full order needs one hundred thirty screws across floor and ramp together.
Three boxes cover it with twenty screws spare on the fifty to a box rule.
Day three then covers the floor laying and day four the ramp build and final checks.
Does the four day plan leave any slack if the treatment needs longer to dry?
base: The brake lines run along the nearside chassis rail, tucked just under the floor edge.
Lever against the crossmembers, never against the rails, and the lines stay out of harm.
Number each board with chalk as it comes out, so the pattern goes back the same way.
Keep the old ramp springs until the new ones are on, in case a horse must travel.
Would your neighbour take the far end of each board while you work the bar?

a: Set the treatment drying time at twenty-four hours before any board is fixed down.
The strip down takes one day and the frame check takes one day as planned.
Move the ramp build to the Friday morning and keep Thursday free as slack.
Write the plan as five short lines, one line for each working day in order.
Close the sheet with the timber line, the screw line, and the day plan together.
base: He will take the far end gladly, and he is steadier with a bar than I am.
We will chalk the boards and keep the old springs wrapped in the barn.
The yard rang to say the treated boards arrive on Thursday with the springs.
That puts the laying on the weekend, which suits the pair of us far better.
The horses can stay out at grass all week, so nothing needs to travel anywhere.

a: Line one reads Monday strip down, and line two reads Tuesday frame check and treatment.
Line three reads Wednesday drying until the new boards can be fixed late in the afternoon.
Line four reads Thursday floor laying with the whole day kept loose as agreed slack.
Line five reads Friday ramp build, with the new springs going on before the boards.
The sheet closes at four hundred eighty-eight pounds of timber and one hundred thirty screws.
base: Then you have a clean week, with the strip at the weekend and laying when the timber lands.
Treat every cut end twice, because the saw opens fresh timber that the yard never touched.
Grease the hinge line while the ramp is bare, since you will never reach it this well again.
When the last board is down, walk the floor slowly and listen for any movement.
A floor that stays silent under your boots will stay silent under the horses.
